A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Ferret and provide readable methods, equations, results, figures, and complete proof and experimental appendices. Content can be matched across the restructuring and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original Ferret evaluations on Natural Instructions and Dolly-15K, plus reconstruction simulations and ablations in Appendix C.

after.justification: v3 retains original Ferret results and adds code-generation and mathematical-reasoning evaluations, memory measurements, and further ablations.

M1.justification: First-order local updates, seeded random projections, block-wise reconstruction, and aggregation remain unchanged in Equations 2–8. Algorithm 1 now names the central server as the transmission recipient, consistent with server communication already described in v1 Appendix C.2; this does not establish a new procedure. Optimizer flexibility and adaptive allocation were already proposed.

E1.justification: v3 adds evaluated code-generation and mathematical-reasoning tasks through CodeAlpaca and GSM8K, alongside the retained Natural Instructions and Dolly-15K evaluations. This substantially broadens the represented tasks beyond the original instruction-tuning experiments.

E2.justification: The seven baselines in Table 2 are retained. FedAvg is newly included in the corresponding convergence comparison, expanding v1 Figure 1's Ferret–FedKSeed comparison to three methods in v3 Figure 2. Extending existing baselines to new datasets does not itself introduce new comparison methods.

E3.justification: v3 adds LLaMA2-7B/13B, LLaMA3-8B, and Qwen2.5-7B configurations, with 20-round code/math evaluations, nine language-based code clients, and three IID GSM8K clients. Appendix C.2 changes FedZO's timing setup from 20 steps with 25 perturbations to 200 steps with one perturbation, and cost reporting shifts from whole-training totals to per-round costs. Peak GPU memory is also evaluated. CodeAlpaca's precise training fraction is ambiguously stated.

E4.justification: v3 adds focused ablations comparing uniform, dimension-based, and update-norm-based allocation of random bases (Figure 4), and Adam versus SGD (Figure 9). Existing reconstruction, K, and block-count analyses remain; moving the latter analyses into the main text does not make them new experiments.

E5.justification: Both versions report Table 2 accuracy as mean ± standard deviation over four runs with different random seeds. The added accuracy tables follow the same practice, without an increased-run claim or new confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: Table 2 retains all four Ferret entries but replaces several baseline results. For example, FedAvg's Natural Instructions/LLaMA-3B score changes from 27.88 ± 0.75 to 32.11 ± 0.70, now exceeding Ferret's unchanged 30.03 ± 0.99. v3 also adds larger-model accuracy, cost, memory, and ablation results. Timing values are revised under changed settings and accounting, so they should not be read as same-setting performance gains.

T1.justification: The theorems, propositions, and main bounds are retained. Theorem 4 and Appendix B.6 correct the variance assumption from loss to stochastic gradient, while Equations 33–35 restore expectations and clarify rearrangement and averaging over rounds. These are limited mathematical corrections.

C1.justification: The abstract and contribution bullets retain the same central claims: first-order federated full-parameter tuning with shared randomness, reduced communication, efficient computation, fast convergence, and competitive accuracy. Broader supporting experiments do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: v3 attributes its accuracy gap against FedAvg on complex tasks to reconstruction error, discusses higher memory requirements than FedKSeed, and identifies detailed privacy analysis and protective mechanisms as future work. These add substantive qualifications to the retained interpretations.

D1.justification: v3 adds checkpoint identifiers, learning rates and search ranges for the larger-model experiments, explicit disclosure of the update-norm allocation used in evaluations, and CPU gradient storage for some 13B baselines. The implementation URL and most original setup details remain unchanged; relocated settings and prompt templates are not new disclosures.

R1.justification: Appendix A expands the positioning beyond PEFT and shared-randomness methods by adding a substantive comparison with gradient compression, including top-k sparsification, signSGD, and FetchSGD. Section 3.2 also relates block-wise reconstruction to SparseGPT and BAdam. This introduces a previously missing methodological comparison category.

P1.justification: The overall section sequence and much of the method and theory prose remain intact. Revisions concentrate on related work and experiments: Section 5 gains subsections, existing FL settings and K/block-count ablations move into the main text, and Appendix C reorganizes setup and prompt descriptions. Author affiliations and publication text are also updated.

P2.justification: v3 adopts a two-column main layout, boxed theoretical statements, and redesigned prompt displays. It adds an overview figure and several result tables and ablation figures, relocates existing ablations, redraws reconstruction plots, and restructures cost tables around per-round reporting. These substantially change the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: Larger-model code/math evaluations, memory measurements, and targeted ablations improve support for scalability and make practical tradeoffs clearer. However, v3 still claims to beat all Natural Instructions baselines despite Table 2 reporting FedAvg at 32.11 versus Ferret at 30.03 on LLaMA-3B; some Section 5.2 speedup claims also disagree with Tables 4–5. These reporting inconsistencies limit the net benefit of the expanded evidence.
